# The public record {#the-public-record .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 4
:::

::: notes
This section puts the morning together. SCORE kept everything that it did with each paper in one public tree of projects on the OSF, and the robustness study left its records in the same trees and in a public dataset of its own. Reading such a record is a skill in itself, which you practise on the record of your own case study, and we end on the route by which you would deposit a reanalysis of your own, so that it leaves a record of the same kind.
:::

::: notes
Each paper selected by SCORE has a project on the OSF, named by a code built from the first author, the journal, the year and a short identifier, with one component for each kind of work done on the paper. The projects of the workshop's two case studies are not alike: the Housing project holds a reproduction that was planned and never carried out, and the Europeanisation project two failed reproductions beside its replication. [advance] The processed results of every reanalysis of the robustness study, the answers to both tasks with the effect sizes converted to the common scale, are public in a repository of their own.
:::

## Reading a dossier {#reading-a-dossier .questionslide}

::: {.none .nonincremental}
Open the SCORE project of your workshop's case study. No account is needed.

- Which components does it hold, and which of the three Rs does each one test?
- Open the component of the robustness study, with Multi100 in its title, and one analyst inside it: what did the analyst leave behind?
- Find the replication: does it have a preregistration, and is the plan dated before the report?
:::

::: notes
Now you read a record yourselves. Open the SCORE project of your case study, from the addresses on the previous slide; everything there is public, and you need no account. Work through the three questions in order: first which components are there and which of the three Rs each one tests, then one analyst of the robustness study, in the component with Multi100 in its title, and whether the analyst left code, data, a report or all three, and last the replication, whose preregistration and report you find and compare by their dates. [state the time] When we compare what you found, the differences between the records show how far each kind of check could go in your case study. [wait]
:::

## Depositing a reanalysis of your own {#depositing-a-reanalysis}

::: {.small .fs-85}
1. **The code goes on a forge**, with a licence file and a README that says what the repository is
2. **Each version that you cite is archived** by a release on Zenodo, which gives it a DOI
3. **The data go where their licence allows.** Public-domain data travel with the code, and data that may not be passed on stay on your machine, with a README that says how to obtain them
4. **The plan goes on OSF Registries** before the analysis runs, with the DOIs of the code and data in its Resources fields
5. **The rendered report is part of the release**, so that the numbers shown are those that the code produced
6. **The data are cited** with their version and the date of download
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Reproducibility repositories of the case-study websites, last section.
:::

::: notes
The session gives a route for depositing a reanalysis such as the one that you build in this workshop, a route that works after the change at the OSF as well as before it. The code goes on a forge, with a licence and a README, and each version that you want to cite is archived on Zenodo, which gives it a DOI. The data go where their licence allows, so that the file of the Housing case study can travel with the code while the Eurobarometer files never leave your machine. The plan is registered before the analysis runs, with links to the archived code and data, the rendered report goes into the release, and the data are cited with their versions. The module on Git and GitHub on the workshop's website takes you through the first two steps.
:::
